role: Junior Composites Process Engineer at a Composites Plant
headline: Fresh out of a bachelor's in composite materials engineering and posted to a composites plant in Wujin, Changzhou: a junior process engineer who spends the day minding a pultrusion line and an autoclave with an old process man, and the evening back in a rented room with a mechanics of composites textbook
unit: A composites plant in Wujin, Changzhou, making carbon-fiber spar-cap plank for wind turbine blades, plus carbon-fiber parts for drones and cars
unit_type: Private composites manufacturer (three to four hundred staff)
education: Bachelor's degree in composite materials engineering
level: You have studied cure chemistry, laminate mechanics and vacuum infusion in the textbooks, and you are quick in SolidWorks. But you can't yet seal a vacuum bag tight, you can't tell a delamination from noise on a C-scan, and you can't explain why each temperature on the process card is the number it is.
intro: You studied composite materials engineering in Wuhan, and your graduation internship was at a wind blade plant, where you watched a blade more than eighty meters long being lifted out of its mold. This composites plant in Wujin, Changzhou, offered you a job with a dorm bed, not too far from home. As of today, you learn under Old Qian on the shop floor, starting with one pultrusion line and one autoclave.
salary_note: Estimate: private composites plants in Wujin start graduate process engineers at roughly the national average, with housing and a night-shift allowance. In years of rush wind installations the bonus is big; in years when blade prices fall it shrinks.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Leading real-time monitoring and intervention during the first-article RTM infusion of a fairing

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Tracing whitish porosity defects in molded fairings and tuning the cure parameters

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 31 related listings nationwide, 0 in this city (mostly campus hiring and internships)

day: In the locker room you pull on your coveralls, mask and nitrile gloves, and turn once in the air shower before entering the layup room. The gauge on the wall reads twenty-two degrees, fifty percent humidity.

On the pultrusion line, glossy black carbon plank inches out of the die. Old Qian has you note the three die-zone temperatures and the puller speed every hour. What you're writing down isn't numbers, he says, it's this plank's temper.

Quality calls: on the ultrasonic C-scan one stretch of plank is the wrong color. You run over to look. Old Qian takes one glance, says delamination, and sends you back to check the die temperatures for that half hour.

Over at the autoclave they are bagging a batch of drone arms. You crouch by the tool watching the vacuum gauge. The five-minute leak check drops a little too far; the operator swears and runs his fingers inch by inch along the sealant tape, feeling for the leak.

In the office you build a layup work instruction from SolidWorks screenshots, marking each ply clearly: zero, plus and minus forty-five, ninety. The shop foreman says there are too many words, the workers won't read it, and tells you to make it one page of pictures.

You go to the freezer for prepreg, and the minus-eighteen air hits your face. You write the time on the issue slip. Old Qian says this roll has been out longer than its out-time allows; even if it still feels soft, it can't be used.
Before leaving you look in on the autoclave control room. Tonight's cure is already running: two degrees a minute up to a hold at one hundred thirty. You set your phone alarm for two in the morning.
Back in your rented room you open the mechanics of composites textbook and sketch fiber and resin in the margin, trying to understand which ply a delamination starts from.

ladder.title: Junior Composites Process Engineer
ladder.focus: Under a mentor, support one step of a process at a time: writing SOPs, keeping production records, simple defect analysis. Passing hands-on assessments in three processes is the key to promotion.

ladder.title: Composites Process Engineer
ladder.focus: Own the full process development of one or two products, from lab trial to volume production, lead process validation and solve eighty percent of floor defects. An AS9100 internal auditor certificate or a CSWA is a hard threshold.

ladder.title: Senior Composites Process Engineer
ladder.focus: Lead process coordination across plants and suppliers, drive standardization and automation upgrades, and close out major quality problems. Requires DOE, simulation and quality systems all three.

ladder.title: Principal Process Engineer / Process Expert
ladder.focus: Set the company's process strategy (such as a roadmap to thermoplastics), review critical process changes and carry responsibility for airworthiness compliance. Holds both technical decision rights and control of project resources.

ai_tasks.name: Tracing whitish porosity defects in molded fairings and tuning the cure parameters
ai_tasks.how: AI can line up the cure curves, bag pressures, prepreg batches and layup records, list likely root causes and an order to check them in, and help make a first call from photos of the part. A person has to go to the floor, look at the part, check what was actually done, find the real cause, and decide how to change the cure parameters and how to error-proof it.

ai_tasks.name: Calibrating cure-kinetics parameters by DSC for a new prepreg batch
ai_tasks.how: AI can largely take this over: processing the DSC curves automatically, fitting the cure-kinetics model, outputting a k(T) function that loads into PAM-RTM and writing the report. A person only needs to spot-check the fit, the odd batches and the agreement with past data, then sign the release.

ai_tasks.name: Leading real-time monitoring and intervention during the first-article RTM infusion of a fairing
ai_tasks.how: AI can help read sensor data, estimate the flow front from simulation and raise early warnings. But within a forty-five-minute window, a racetracking flow or a stalled front has to be judged and handled by a person on the spot, working the valves and changing the injection strategy, and if it goes wrong a person answers for it. This one rests mainly on people.

ai_tasks.name: Writing the compression-molding process card, with PFMEA, for a drone wing skin
ai_tasks.how: AI can draft the card from a template, generate a first PFMEA from similar parts and check formatting and consistency. A person has to set the process route and key parameters around the double-curved layup, the mold and the actual equipment, review the PFMEA's severity and risk ranking, and answer for the controlled document.

ai_tasks.name: Quickly diagnosing and closing out cracking at demolding after autoclave cure
ai_tasks.how: AI can quickly pull together the cure curves, tool and layup data and similar past cracking cases, list hypotheses and draft the 8D or countermeasure report. A person has to go look at the fracture surface, check the corner plies and the demolding practice, confirm the root cause, decide whether a temporary fix can release production, and answer for the permanent countermeasure.

ai_tasks.name: Analyzing and validating a cost-down BOM for HP-RTM on a satellite bracket
ai_tasks.how: AI can break down BOM costs, compare materials and resin options, run sensitivity on cycle time and draft the test plan. A person has to judge whether the T800 and BMI systems are workable for the process window, the equipment's HP-RTM temperature and pressure limits and customer qualification, lead the validation trials, and explain the trade-offs to the customer and management.

events.e_bag_leak: On a night shift a vacuum bag you sealed leaks halfway through the cure, and a whole autoclave load of drone arms comes out white and scrapped. The next day Old Qian has you strip the bag with him and hunt for the leak inch by inch. You find it: a fold in the sealant tape that was never pressed down.
events.e_first_part: The first batch of RTM car parts made to a plan you wrote yourself comes back with a clean first-article C-scan, not a single dry spot. You print the scan and slip it under the glass on your desk.
events.e_wind_rush: Wind power hits an installation rush, and spar-cap orders are booked six months out. The pultrusion lines run three shifts, you get two days off in a month, and the month-end bonus is double the usual.
events.e_price_war: The turbine makers squeeze price after price, and blade prices fall thirty percent in two years. The plant cuts the year-end bonus and asks each of you for one cost-down measure a month. You rework the offcut nesting plan three times.
events.e_allergy: A red rash spreads across your wrist, itching too much to sleep. The doctor says it's a contact allergy to epoxy. From then on you wear two pairs of gloves and wrap tape around your cuffs.
events.e_scrap: A batch of spar-cap resin gels too early and hundreds of meters of carbon plank set hard inside the die. Stopping the line and clearing the die takes three days, and the loss is more than you earn in several years. The root cause turns out to be a drum of hardener stored in the wrong place. Your 8D report runs to eleven pages.
events.e_audit: A drone manufacturer comes to audit. The auditor picks a process card at random and asks why the cure hold is ninety minutes. You pull out the DSC curves and three validation records and walk him through them line by line. He puts a tick in his notebook.
events.e_dsc_ai: DSC calibration of new prepreg batches is now fitted automatically by software, kinetics parameters and report in minutes. It used to take you an afternoon of calculation. Now you just spot-check the fitted curve against past batches and sign.
events.e_ai_wrong: For a whitish porosity problem, the AI lines up cure curves, bag pressures and material batches and ranks the resin batch as the top cause. You spend two shifts crouched on the floor and find the night shift has a new layup worker who isn't compacting the plies properly.
events.e_databank: The plant is building a process data platform, and you match ten years of autoclave curves, C-scans and defect logs to their batch numbers one by one and load them in. It takes most of a year. From then on, if anyone asks what went wrong with which load, it's one click away.
events.e_patent: A new way you devised of laying the flow mesh halves the dry spots on large infusions. The company files it as a utility model patent, your name first among the inventors, with a two-thousand-yuan bonus.
events.e_midnight: At three in the morning the autoclave throws an overtemperature alarm and the duty phone rings you. You ride your e-bike back to the plant in ten minutes and change the thermocouple with the maintenance tech. The load is saved, and it's already light.
events.e_dust: You stand in the grinding room watching workers trim the edges of a batch of carbon parts, black dust drifting in the light. You cough for a week afterward, and go to your manager to get the extraction hoods replaced.
events.e_mentor: Old Qian retires, and before he goes he gives you his process notebook from thirty years on the floor. Tucked inside are a few yellowed cure curves, and in a margin he has written: in the plum-rain season, bag it twice.
events.e_title: You are certified at the intermediate engineer title. At the review interview they ask the difference between pultrusion and filament winding. You talk for ten minutes, and end with the autoclave load you scrapped.
events.e_expo: At a composites show in Shanghai, the biggest crowd is around the thermoplastics stands: no freezers, weldable, recyclable. You stand in front of an automated tape-laying machine for half an hour and take dozens of photos.
events.e_wedding: You get married, to a colleague who runs inspection in the quality department. The banquet is at a hotel in Wujin. Old Qian has too much to drink and tells the bride that whenever you two argue, settle it with a C-scan.
events.e_house: You buy a three-bedroom in Wujin New Town, with five years of savings for the down payment plus what both sets of parents pooled. On handover day you walk through the bare concrete rooms; the floor is all dust.
events.e_child: The night your child is born you are still on the floor waiting for a load to come out of the autoclave. The nurse calls. You shove the record sheet at the shift leader and race to the hospital on your e-bike, running a yellow light on the way.
events.e_trainee: The plant runs a field-engineer class with a vocational college and assigns you two diploma students. Like Old Qian once did, you have them spend a month in the layup room first, writing no documents at all.
events.e_knees: After more than twenty years on your feet on the shop floor, your knees start creaking on the stairs. You cut your trips to the floor from three a day to two, and for the third you have your apprentice send you video.
events.e_recycle: The first decommissioned blades come back, and the plant tries shredding them into manhole covers and board. Standing by the shredder, you recognize a length of spar cap you made years ago, the batch number still legible.

c_floor.title: Six months rotating through the production line first
c_floor.situation: Your manager says new process engineers can spend six months rotating through layup, bagging, demolding and grinding, working alongside the operators and doing night shifts. Or you can stay in the technical office writing documents and following Old Qian around the floor. People who rotate spot problems faster afterward, but for those six months you produce almost nothing of your own.

options.label: Rotate, starting with layup
options.result: For six months the resin smell won't wash off your hands, and you bag until you can feel a fold with your eyes shut. Back in the office, when you write an SOP, the first step you write is the one where operators are most likely to slip.

options.label: Stay in the office and write documents
options.result: You reorganize more than forty of the plant's old process cards, with one format and aligned revisions. On the floor, though, you still have to jot down the operators' slang and look it up afterward.

c_as9100.title: Take the AS9100D internal auditor exam and go for Composites Process Engineer
c_as9100.situation: There are more and more drone and aerospace customers, and the plant needs someone who knows the aerospace quality system. Your manager says that with an AS9100D internal auditor certificate, you'd get first pick when it's time to own a product line. The course is a week in Nanjing, the exam means memorizing a thick book of clauses, and you pay half the fee yourself.

options.label: Sign up and study clauses on weekends
options.result: You paper the wall of your rented room with clause numbers, and your palms are wet on exam day. Once the certificate comes through, your first internal audit turns up three old process cards that were never under document control.

options.label: Skip it for now and master the floor
options.result: You spend that week on the filament-winding line, making samples of every kind of defect. Later the aerospace customer's orders go to a colleague on the next team who had the certificate.

c_line.title: The wind line or the drone line
c_line.situation: The plant has opened a new line for carbon-fiber parts for drones and low-altitude aircraft, and it needs process engineers. Wind spar caps are high-volume and steady, and you already know them; the new line is small batches, lots of part numbers, drawings changing every day. But the owner says low-altitude flight is where the future is.

options.label: Go to the new drone line
options.result: In one month you write a dozen new process cards, compression molding, autoclave and RTM in turn. The customer's structural engineers message you at midnight to change the layup, and you learn to ask first: once it changes, who signs?

options.label: Stay on wind spar caps
options.result: You bring the pultrusion scrap rate down from three percent to one point two, and the plant manager names you at the monthly meeting. Life is level and steady, and every day you look at the same glossy black plank.

c_ai_data.title: Should you take on the process data and AI analysis?
c_ai_data.situation: The owner has hired a software company to build AI process analysis, and it needs someone who knows the process to work alongside: labeling cure curves and defect records correctly, reviewing the root causes and parameter suggestions the AI produces. It isn't part of your performance targets, and it would take a good share of your time.

options.label: Take it and learn to work with data
options.result: You learn to pull a year of cure curves onto one chart in Python. The AI's first suggestions are half wrong; you annotate them one by one and send them back, and the second version is far more sensible.

options.label: Decline and stay on the floor
options.result: You say the floor keeps you busy enough. The software company assigns a younger colleague as liaison, and now and then you're called into a meeting to explain why a curve can't be read that way.

c_liyang.title: A battery plant in Liyang comes headhunting
c_liyang.situation: A power battery plant in Liyang is hiring smart-manufacturing process engineers to manage the process parameters and equipment data on cell lines, and your work on process data has caught their eye. Thirty-five percent more pay, mostly day shifts, no resin smell. But it's a different trade, and most of what you know about composites won't apply.

options.label: Go to the battery plant
options.result: You hand your coveralls back to the stores and walk through the layup room one last time.
options.end: You go to Liyang, and from then on your world is cells and electrodes. Years later, driving past Wujin, you can still pick out the composites plant's chimney through the car window, and remember the fold your fingers found in a vacuum bag.

options.label: Stay in composites
options.result: You turn the headhunter down and spend that afternoon as usual beside the autoclave, watching a first article. When it comes out, the surface is glossy enough to reflect your mask.

c_doe.title: Lead a quality close-out and go for Senior Composites Process Engineer
c_doe.situation: A car customer's carbon parts are warping across a whole batch, and they want it closed out within three months. Whoever leads has to run a full DOE, bring in PAM-RTM simulation, change the tooling and hold weekly meetings with the customer, which is exactly what the Senior Composites Process Engineer review looks at. For those three months you would have almost no weekends.

options.label: Lead it and close it in three months
options.result: You run sixteen trial sets, and the simulated dry-spot locations match the real ones more than eighty percent of the time. At the last weekly meeting the customer's quality manager says it is the cleanest close-out report he has ever seen.

options.label: Take only the simulation part
options.result: Your manager leads; you handle the simulation and do it beautifully. At the year-end review, your name is on page two of the report.

c_shanghai.title: A post at a Shanghai airliner supplier
c_shanghai.situation: A composites supplier to the big airliner program in Shanghai is hiring process engineers for fuselage panels and fairings: you'd need to know airworthiness and keep every controlled autoclave document straight. Over twenty percent more pay, but your home is in Changzhou and your child has just started primary school, so you could only come back on weekends.

options.label: Go to Shanghai, home on weekends
options.result: Every Monday you take the train a little after six to Shanghai and come back Friday night. When the airworthiness reviewers come they stay a week, and you learn that every number must trace back to an original record.

options.label: Stay in Changzhou
options.result: You don't go. On weekends you take your child to the dinosaur park, and on Monday you're back in the layup room as usual. You print the airworthiness requirements from that job ad and check your own plant's documents against them one by one.

c_expert.title: Go for Principal Process Engineer / Process Expert
c_expert.situation: The plant has to set a roadmap for moving to thermoplastics, and the owner wants a Principal Process Engineer / Process Expert in the technical department to review every critical process change and answer for customer qualification. It means presenting a plan to the technical committee, and if you get it, every word you sign is yours to answer for.

options.label: Present a plan and go for it
options.result: Your roadmap runs three years in three steps, the first being to switch a single part from thermoset to thermoplastic. At the review the owner asks how much it will cost. You give him a number, then the worst-case number.

options.label: Don't apply; stay on the floor and train people
options.result: You recommend a colleague who has come back from Shanghai. You still go into the layup room every day, and your apprentices say that when you walk past, the operators slow down half a beat and work more carefully.

c_own.title: Go into business with your old shift leader
c_own.situation: Your old shift leader from the pultrusion line has gone out on his own making composite molds and fixtures in Wujin, with more orders than he can handle, and he wants you in: you bring the technology, he brings the money and the crew. A small shop has no company annuity and no professional titles; you live from one order to the next.

options.label: Join him and go it alone
options.result: Your resignation letter is two lines long. You take out the C-scan that sat under your desk glass for so many years.
options.end: You and your old shift leader run the little shop in a row of factory units in Wujin for many years, making blade molds and drone fixtures. A handwritten sign hangs by the gate. Every morning you're the first one in, and the first thing you do is lay a hand on the molds to feel how warm they are.

options.label: Stay at the plant
options.result: You introduce your old shift leader to two customers but stay put. At every holiday he still turns up with a crate of oranges and says people like you can't live without a big autoclave.

endings.retire: On your last day you don't go into the layup room. You stand at the door of the air shower and watch the young engineers turn in it one by one and go in. You leave your process notebook to your apprentice, with Old Qian's curves inside and your own as well. As you walk out the gate, another length of carbon plank is easing out of the die on the pultrusion line.
endings.burnout: That year your allergy and your cough flare up together, and the doctor says no more shop floor. The plant moves you to the archive to sort decades of process cards and C-scans. You leave on time every day, and when you pass the autoclave you still stop to look at the curve on the control screen.

stages: You mind a pultrusion line and an autoclave with Old Qian, writing production records every day, copying cure curves, photographing and numbering every scrapped part. When quality brings a C-scan, you go look at the part on the floor first and then check the records in the office. Layup workers ask their shift leader first and come to you only when he isn't sure. You can draft documents, but signing isn't yours yet.

You own one or two products from lab trial to volume production: you set the layup and the cure window, run tool trials and process validation, and your name is on the process cards and the PFMEA. You can call eighty percent of floor defects on the spot, and the customer's structural engineers, the tooling shop and the prepreg supplier all come straight to you. You start learning to say in meetings: this can't be changed.

What you manage now is how the process lines up across several plants and suppliers: which line gets automated fiber placement, which defect gets a formal close-out project, how the standard documents are unified. You work with DOE in one hand, simulation in another and the quality system in a third, with three or four process engineers under you. You go to the floor less, and sit in more review meetings and customer calls.

You set the plant's process direction for the next ten years: whether to move from thermosets to thermoplastics, whether critical process changes are approved, who carries the compliance documents for aerospace customers. Most of what you read every day is other people's plans and reports, and you go to the floor to see one key first article. At the technical committee you are often the last to speak, and you say the least.
work: Sun, the shift leader, says the edge of today's prepreg roll feels a little stiff. You check the freezer issue log and find the last shift didn't put it back in time; it sat out four extra hours. The roll goes back.

You seal a vacuum bag on a large part by yourself for the first time, and in the five-minute leak check it barely drops. Old Qian crouches and runs the back of his hand along the tape all the way round, then stands up: fine, in it goes.
Quality brings a C-scan with white patches. You match the batch number to that load's cure curve and find a three-degree dip during the hold; it traces back to a loose thermocouple.
A drone customer cuts the arm layup from twelve plies to ten. You redo the ply book in SolidWorks, send three tensile coupons for testing, and sign the change order only after the data passes.

Thirty minutes into an RTM infusion on a car part, the flow front stalls at a corner. You have the operator close one injection port and open another, the front starts moving again, and that part is saved.

A new prepreg supplier delivers a first batch. You run DSC and gel time to spec and find the gel time two minutes shorter than the old supplier's, so you go back and slow the ramp rate on the process card.

You take two process engineers to benchmark a partner plant in Nantong. Same spar-cap plank, double your scrap rate, and the problem is in the preheat zone of their pultrusion die. You leave them your parameter sheet.

At a review meeting a young engineer wants to cut twenty minutes from the cure to save cost. You don't veto it. You have him run a four-factor, two-level DOE first and come back with the Minitab results.

A customer complains that a batch cracked after demolding. On the call you don't apologize first; you ask for photos of the fracture surface, and after looking you say it's the overlap of the corner plies. Three days later you deliver the 8D report.

On the first trial of a thermoplastic part, you stand by the welding machine all afternoon watching an operator induction-weld two panels into one. Back in the office you put a tick after step one of the roadmap.

An aerospace customer is doing an airworthiness compliance review. You go through the autoclave self-check list item by item, and on the day the reviewers come you just sit in the meeting room and let the young engineers present.

The process department submits a change from vacuum infusion to compression molding that would save thirty percent of labor hours. You go through twenty years of defect logs and approve it, with one condition: every part gets C-scanned for the first three months.
past: You go to middle school in Xuancheng, Anhui. In your hometown there's a small workshop that makes fiberglass fishing boats, and after school you often go watch them brush on resin and lay glass cloth, the whole place full of a sharp, stinging smell.

Your gaokao (college entrance exam) score is middling. Leafing through the admissions catalog you see composite materials engineering, think of that workshop, and put down the program at an engineering university in Wuhan.

In your second-year design project your group makes a carbon panel by vacuum infusion. The vacuum leaks three times, and the panel you end up with is full of bubbles. The teacher says this is how you'll be earning your living.

Your graduation internship is at a wind blade plant in Yancheng, where you see a blade mold more than eighty meters long for the first time, with dozens of workers laying cloth in it at once. You fill a notebook with where the flow mesh and breather go.

In campus hiring you get offers from an aerospace research institute and from this composites plant in Changzhou. At the institute you'd need a master's to move up; the plant gives you a dorm bed and is two hours' drive from home. You sign with Changzhou.

late.pension_note: Estimate: private manufacturers in Changzhou mostly pay pension contributions on a middling share of actual wages, with no company annuity, so the basic pension comes to about half your last monthly pay.
scenes: In your first month of retirement you still wake at 7:20 and reach for the mask on the nightstand. What your hand finds is your reading glasses. You put them on and look at the weather on your phone a while.
The plant brings you back as an adviser a few days a month to look over the new lines' process cards. On one card you draw a circle, and beside it write: in the plum-rain season, bag it twice.

On the open ground below your building you help a neighbor repair a little fiberglass boat, two pairs of gloves on while you brush the resin. A child upstairs leans out of the window watching all afternoon.
You and your spouse drive to the coast at Yancheng, where rows of turbines are turning in the distance. You point at one and say the spar cap in that blade might be one of ours.
The archive is quiet. You scan decades of C-scans into the system one by one, and when you come to the first load you ever scrapped, the white patch on it is still glaring.
Once you're off the floor the rash on your wrist slowly fades, and you stop coughing at night. Every evening you walk along the Grand Canal and turn back at the bridge by the old factory district.
On the day you file your retirement papers, HR asks if you'd like to look around the shop floor once more. You say no need, and stand a moment outside the air shower, listening to the wind inside.
In the first year in another trade, the smell of paint from a neighbor's renovation still has you guessing, without meaning to, which resin it is.
On an errand in Wujin you stop by your old plant's gate. The guard is new and won't let you in. Standing there, you see a new row of solar panels on the pultrusion hall's roof.
The apprentice you trained has become a principal process engineer. He sends you a photo: the notebook with Old Qian's curves in it, now with a thick new stack of pages added.

Your child's school visits a renewable energy exhibition, and afterward your child tells you about seeing a huge wind blade. You ask what color it was. White, your child says. You say: inside, it's black.

The first blades you made spar caps for are decommissioned, and the news says they were shredded and laid into a road. Out on a walk, you stand on the newly paved sidewalk and look down at it for a while.

closing.retire: Many years later, one evening, you sit on a bench by the Grand Canal as the lights of the industrial park come on, block by block. You think of the carbon plank inching out of the die on the pultrusion line: slow, steady, never stopping for a moment.
closing.burnout: Many years later, you are repotting flowers on the balcony, your fingers coated in black soil. You look at them, think of the resin smell that never washed off your hands, smile a little, and press the soil down.
closing.end: Many years later, in an old box, you find a small carbon-fiber sample panel from your college design project, full of bubbles. You turn it in your hand and hold it up to the light a while, then put it back in the box.
